1.summary: How the course is assessed and what it covers, why natural language is hard for machines (ambiguity at every level from morphology to pragmatics), what NLP systems do, how text becomes an evaluated result, and how the field moved from rules to large language models.

facts.d: F1 is the project (oral responses, application demo, written documentation); F2 is the final test on the lecture outcomes, in the final lecture slot. Final grade P = 0.8 F1 + 0.2 F2.

Foundations: classical NLP and text classification, word and text embeddings, LSTMs and the Transformer, large language models. Systems: retrieval-augmented generation, deploying LLMs, visualising text similarity, explainable AI and speech analysis.
"I saw the man with the telescope": who has the telescope? "Zamek był zamknięty": a lock or a castle? The input holds characters and words; the intended meaning stays implicit.
Analyse language (classify texts, find entities, relations and events, retrieve information, recognise speech) and produce it (translate, answer questions, summarise, generate text and speech).

Morphology: how words are formed (work, worked). Syntax: how words combine. Semantics: what an expression means (bank, zamek). Discourse: how sentences connect (Max arrived. He sat down.). Pragmatics: what the speaker intends (I have to work tonight).

facts.t: A token is not always a word
facts.d: "Nie zrobiłbym tego" can be split into characters, tokens, word forms, lemmas or morphemes. The single form zrobiłbym carries a lexical meaning (zrobić), past tense, first person singular and conditional mood.
The same form plays different roles: back door, on my back, win the voters back, back the bill; zamek in a door, on a hill, or as a zip.
"The police officer observed the man with binoculars": the officer used binoculars, or the man carried them. Grammar constrains interpretation but may not resolve it.

Implicature: "Some of them did" suggests not all students passed. Indirect answers: "I have to work" means the speaker will not come. Interpretation may need the situation, shared knowledge and a model of the speaker.

facts.t: From raw text to a result
facts.d: Raw text → segmentation and normalisation → representation (features, embeddings, model states) → model output (label, extracted information, generated text) → evaluation. Errors can start in the data, representation, model or evaluation.

"The battery lasts all day, but the camera is disappointing" supports sentiment analysis (mixed), aspect extraction (battery, camera), aspect sentiment (battery positive, camera negative), summarisation and retrieval. The task decides which meaning must be kept.

A corpus provides authentic language, metadata about sources and speakers, optional annotations and training and evaluation material. Quality depends on domain coverage, balance, annotation consistency and separating training from test data; a larger corpus can still represent the wrong population.

1. Rules and formal grammars. 2. Statistical NLP with probabilistic models from annotated corpora. 3. Neural representations replacing manual features. 4. Transformers and LLMs adapted by prompting or extra training. New methods do not remove ambiguity, data problems or the need to evaluate.

Building the Polish Large Language Model touches every topic of the course: representative corpora, tokenisation and learned representations, the Transformer and training, evaluation and explainability, deployment and retrieval of external knowledge.

traps: Semantics asks what an expression means; pragmatics asks what the speaker intends by saying it.
A token, a word form, a lemma and a morpheme are different units; one Polish word form can carry several grammatical meanings.
Statistical NLP learned from annotated corpora; neural methods learn the representations themselves.

2.summary: Turning raw text into linguistic annotation: extraction and normalisation problems, sentence and token segmentation, subword tokens and offsets, lemmas and lexemes, stemming versus lemmatisation, morphological analysis and tagging, named entities with BIO labels, and lexical meaning in WordNet-style networks.

facts.d: Normalisation (Unicode, spacing, punctuation, numbers), segmentation into sentences and tokens, morphological analysis (lemmas and features), tagging (one interpretation per token), entity recognition (person, location, amount) and lexical semantics (senses and relations).

Hyphenation at line breaks splits words in two; headers, footers, page numbers and footnotes get mixed into the text; OCR or PDF extraction may read across columns. Word counts, sentence boundaries and meaning change.

Two identical-looking "für" strings can differ: NFC stores ü as one code point U+00FC (2 UTF-8 bytes), NFD as u plus a combining diaeresis U+0075 U+0308 (3 bytes). Decode bytes correctly (usually UTF-8), then normalise, commonly to NFC.
Apple vs apple, Polish vs polish; "Let's eat, Grandma!" vs "Let's eat Grandma!". Lowercasing and removing punctuation simplify the vocabulary but can damage meaning and annotations.

A full stop can mark an abbreviation, a decimal number, a URL or the end of a sentence; quotes and brackets can follow it; headlines, chats and transcripts often drop punctuation. Language-specific abbreviation lists help rule-based splitters.

facts.t: A token is a modelling decision
facts.d: don't, New York, e-mail, 12.50, :-), zrobiłbym can each be one token or several: one token keeps an entity or word form; several expose structure (do + n't, zrobił + by + m). Boundaries depend on language, standard and application.

Linguistic tokenisation aims at words and meaningful segments for annotation and corpus search. Model tokenisation splits text into units of a fixed vocabulary to control sequence length and unknown words, e.g. tokenisation = token + isation; it need not follow word boundaries.
Each token stores its start and end position in the source text (Ada = text[0:3]), so annotations stay auditable and results can be highlighted in the original document.

A lexeme is an abstract vocabulary unit with one meaning; the lemma is its dictionary form; a word form occurs in text (kotami, lemma kot). One lemma can name several lexemes: zamek as door lock, castle or zipper.

Stemming shortens words mechanically with affix rules and may produce non-words; it is an information-retrieval baseline. Lemmatisation uses morphology, often context, and returns the dictionary lemma (kobietami → kobieta); the right lemma can depend on context.

A morphological analyser lists all candidate analyses (mam: mama, mieć or mamić) and aims for coverage; a tagger picks the interpretation that fits the context ("Wiele mam nie przyszło": many mothers did not come).
kotami → subst:pl:inst:m2: noun, plural, instrumental, masculine animate. A tagset defines the classes, features, values and legal combinations; corpora of one language may use different tagsets.

The token, its neighbours, affixes, spelling and capitalisation all give evidence (I read a book / Please book a room). The best tag for one token depends on neighbouring decisions, which motivates HMMs, CRFs, recurrent networks and Transformers.
NER finds the span of each mention (mention detection) and assigns it a type (typing): person, organisation, location, date, money. The inventory depends on the application.
B-type begins an entity, I-type continues it, O is outside: New/B-ORG York/I-ORG University/I-ORG hired/O Ada/B-PER. BIO turns span recognition into sequence labelling, like POS tagging.
Boundaries (University of Wrocław, New York Times reporter) and types (Washington: person or place; Amazon: company or river; Jaguar: animal, company or product) can both be ambiguous.

WordNet stores lexical meaning as a graph: nodes are lexical units or synsets with glosses and examples, edges are semantic and lexical relations. Słowosieć is the Polish network, linked with Princeton WordNet.
A synset groups lexical units (senses), not spellings: {idol 1, bożyszcze 1, gwiazdor 1}. The number marks a particular sense; synonymy depends on sense and context.
Organises meanings by generality: body of water is the hypernym of ocean, ocean the hyponym, sea a co-hyponym. Test: an ocean must be a body of water, but not the other way round.
Part–whole relations of several kinds: part (bulb / hair), portion (slice / bread), place (auditorium / cinema), collection element (wild boar / game), material (substance / tissue).
WordNet-style resources give explicit, interpretable knowledge but are costly to build; corpora give frequencies and context but are implicit and biased by the texts collected.

A wrong sentence split changes context, wrong token boundaries confuse the tagger, wrong tags remove evidence, an NER boundary error splits a name, and entity linking then looks for the wrong object. Evaluate end to end.

Search keeps lexical content (don't delete numbers); sentiment keeps emphasis and negation (don't drop punctuation); authorship keeps style (don't correct spelling); entity linking keeps exact mentions (don't lowercase everything).

formulas.name: Unicode forms of ü
formulas.expr: NFC: U+00FC (C3 BC, 2 bytes);  NFD: U+0075 U+0308 (75 CC 88, 3 bytes)

traps: Decoding (bytes to characters) and Unicode normalisation (equivalent character sequences) are separate steps.
Stemming may produce non-words; lemmatisation returns a dictionary form and may need context.
An analyser proposes all readings; a tagger chooses one.
A lemma names a dictionary form; one lemma (zamek) can stand for several lexemes.

3.summary: Classical text classification: supervised learning and losses, honest data splits and leakage, linear classifiers, SVMs and neural networks, metrics from the confusion matrix and the class-imbalance trap, cross-entropy and gradient descent, and how text becomes vectors with one-hot encoding, bag of words and n-grams.

facts.d: Assigns labels to texts: sentiment, spam or legitimate, topic, intent, for reviews, messages, news or queries. The examples define what the model should predict.
Learn a parameterised model fθ from input–label pairs D = {(x1, y1), …, (xn, yn)} so that it predicts useful labels ŷ for examples it did not see in training.
Parameters (weights, biases, coefficients) are learned from training data. Hyperparameters (learning rate, regularisation, number and size of layers) are chosen outside training, with validation.
The loss ℓ(fθ(xi), yi) gives a cost to wrong predictions; training minimises the average L(θ) with an optimiser. Low training loss alone does not guarantee useful predictions on new data.

Training learns parameters; validation chooses hyperparameters, models and stopping time; the test set gives one final estimate on unseen data and is never used for repeated selection. Illustrative split 70 / 15 / 15. Evaluation assumes the same distribution as deployment.

Duplicates across subsets, one author in train and test, or vocabulary and IDF built from non-training documents leak information. Split by author, conversation or source, use a later period as test, fit preprocessing on training data only.

Each class gets a logit zk = wkᵀx + bk; softmax p(y = k | x) = e^zk / Σj e^zj turns them into probabilities that sum to one. Fast, good with sparse high-dimensional vectors, inspectable, a strong TF–IDF baseline.

Among many separating hyperplanes, an SVM prefers the one with the largest margin; support vectors are the examples closest to the boundary. A linear SVM works well with TF–IDF; its raw scores are not probabilities.

For spam as the positive class: TP spam caught, FP legitimate mail blocked, FN spam let through, TN legitimate mail accepted. The positive class must be defined first. Slide example: TP 80, FN 20, FP 10, TN 890.
Accuracy = (TP + TN) / all. Precision = TP / (TP + FP): when it says spam, how often is it right? Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of all spam, how much was found? F1 = 2PR / (P + R).
With 1% fraud, always predicting "not fraud" gives 99% accuracy and 0% fraud recall. Report per-class results; macro averaging weights classes equally, micro averaging favours frequent classes.
z = Σj wj xj + b and a = ϕ(z): inputs, learned weights (importance and direction), a learned offset and an activation function.

Sigmoid 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ) maps to (0, 1), useful for binary outputs; ReLU = max(0, z) is a common, easy-to-optimise hidden activation. Without nonlinearity, stacked linear layers collapse into one linear map.
h(1) = ϕ(W(1)x + b(1)), h(2) = ϕ(W(2)h(1) + b(2)), z = W(3)h(2) + b(3): each layer is an affine map plus a nonlinearity; the final scores z are logits.
Binary: one score with sigmoid (spam / legitimate). Multiclass: one score per class with softmax (one topic). Multilabel: one score per label, each with its own sigmoid (several tags).
ℓCE = −Σ yk log pk = −log py. For py = 0.9, 0.5, 0.1 it gives 0.105, 0.693, 2.303, against squared errors of 0.010, 0.250, 0.810: confident mistakes are punished much harder.

Forward pass to logits and probabilities, loss against the label, backpropagation by the chain rule from output to input, optimiser updates every weight θ ← θ − η∇L(θ), and validation decides which checkpoint to keep.
Classifiers need fixed-size numeric input, but text is variable-length discrete symbols. The representation decides which distinctions the classifier can use; it is part of the model design.
Each vocabulary item gets its own dimension; different words are orthogonal, so one-hot encoding has no notion of similar meanings.

Counts vocabulary terms per document: each column a feature, each row a fixed-size document vector. It keeps presence and frequency but loses word order, so "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same.
Word bigrams (is not, not good) keep local order and negation; character n-grams (cam, amer) tolerate spelling variation and expose affixes. More context, but a much larger vocabulary.

Tokenisation defines candidate terms; minimum and maximum frequency and a size limit control the feature space. Lemma-based TF–IDF merges kot, kota, kotem into one feature. Build vocabulary and thresholds from training documents only.

formulas.name: Softmax
formulas.expr: p(y = k | x) = e^zk / Σj e^zj

traps: The validation set chooses models and stopping time; the test set is used once at the end.
Precision looks at predicted positives; recall looks at actual positives.
Softmax for mutually exclusive classes; a separate sigmoid per label for multilabel tasks.
Bag of words keeps counts but loses order; n-grams bring back only local order.

questions.q: How is the final grade P computed in this course?
questions.hint: F1 is the project; the test weighs less.
questions.r: Slide 5: F1 is the project assessment, F2 the final test; P = 0.8 F1 + 0.2 F2.

questions.q: "I have to work tonight" given as an answer to an invitation is a matter of which level?
questions.hint: What does the speaker intend by saying it?
questions.r: Slide 17: pragmatics asks what the speaker intends; semantics asks what an expression means. The indirect answer means the speaker will not come.

questions.q: Which level asks how words are formed, as in work, works, worked?
questions.hint: Word structure, not sentence structure.
questions.r: Slide 17: morphology studies word formation; syntax how words combine; discourse how sentences connect; pragmatics the speaker's intention.

questions.q: "The police officer observed the man with binoculars" is an example of:
questions.hint: Who holds the binoculars?
questions.r: Slide 20: the phrase "with binoculars" can attach to the officer's action or to the man; grammar constrains but does not resolve it.

questions.q: Asked "Did all students pass?", someone answers "Some of them did." What does a typical listener infer?
questions.hint: Why would the speaker say "some" if "all" were true?
questions.r: Slide 21: an implicature; the listener infers that not all students passed, although the words alone do not say so.

questions.q: Which grammatical information is packed into the single Polish word form zrobiłbym?
o: Past tense, first person singular and conditional mood
Future tense, third person plural and imperative mood
Present tense, second person singular and passive voice
Infinitive form, no person, and the indicative mood
questions.hint: "I would have done".
questions.r: Slide 18: zrobiłbym carries the lexical meaning zrobić plus past tense, first person singular and conditional mood: a token is not always a word.

questions.q: Which statement about corpora matches the lecture?
o: A larger corpus may still represent the wrong population
A larger corpus always gives a better model in any domain
Annotation consistency matters less than corpus size
Training and test data may freely share documents
questions.hint: Coverage and balance matter, not only size.
questions.r: Slide 24: quality depends on domain coverage, balance, annotation consistency and separating training from test data; size alone does not fix the wrong population.

questions.q: In which stage of NLP were probabilistic models estimated from annotated corpora?
questions.hint: The second of the four stages.
questions.r: Slide 25: 1. rules and grammars, 2. statistical NLP with probabilistic models from annotated corpora, 3. neural representations replacing manual features, 4. Transformers and LLMs.

questions.q: Which sequence matches the path from raw text to an evaluated result?
questions.hint: Prepare the text, encode it, predict, then judge.
questions.r: Slide 22: raw text → segmentation and normalisation → representation (features, embeddings, states) → model output → evaluation.

questions.q: Name the five levels of linguistic context from the lecture, with the main question and an example for each.
questions.a:
- Morphology: how are words formed? work, works, worked.
- Syntax: how do words combine? Who used the telescope?
- Semantics: what does the expression mean? bank, zamek.
- Discourse: how do sentences connect? Max arrived. He sat down.
- Pragmatics: what does the speaker intend? I have to work tonight.

questions.q: Two strings "für" look identical, but one is 3 bytes longer in UTF-8 terms of ü. What is going on?
o: One uses NFC, the other NFD
One uses ASCII, the other UTF-8
One was lowercased, the other not
One contains a hidden line break
questions.hint: Precomposed vs decomposed characters.
questions.r: Slide 4: NFC stores ü as U+00FC (2 bytes), NFD as u + combining diaeresis U+0075 U+0308 (3 bytes). Decode first, then normalise, commonly to NFC.

questions.q: Why can lowercasing and removing punctuation be harmful?
o: They can change meaning and annotation quality
They make the vocabulary larger and sparser
They are slow on long documents
They break UTF-8 decoding of the text
questions.hint: Polish vs polish; Let's eat, Grandma!
questions.r: Slide 5: they simplify the vocabulary but can damage meaning (Apple vs apple, Polish vs polish, Let's eat, Grandma!) and annotation quality.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a language model's subword tokeniser?
o: Control sequence length and unknown words with a fixed vocabulary
Reproduce the linguistic word boundaries of each language
Mark each word with its part of speech and lemma
Remove punctuation and normalise Unicode characters
questions.hint: tokenisation = token + isation.
questions.r: Slide 8: model tokenisation splits text into units from a fixed vocabulary, controlling sequence length and unknown words; it need not follow linguistic word boundaries.

questions.q: Why do annotation tools store character offsets for every token?
o: To keep results auditable and highlight them in the source
To compress the text into fewer bytes for storage
To translate the tokens into another language
To guarantee that tokens never cross word boundaries
questions.hint: Ada = text[0:3].
questions.r: Slide 9: offsets connect annotations with the original text, making them auditable and allowing results to be highlighted in the document.

questions.q: zamek can mean door lock, castle or zipper. In the lecture's terms, this is:
o: one word form with several stems
questions.hint: The dictionary form is shared; the meanings differ.
questions.r: Slide 10: a lemma is the dictionary form naming a lexeme; the spelling and lemma zamek are shared, but each meaning is a different lexeme.

questions.q: How does stemming differ from lemmatisation?
o: It cuts affixes by rule and may not return a real word
It uses context to choose the correct dictionary form
It returns the lemma together with grammatical tags
It works only for Polish and never for English
questions.hint: A heuristic baseline for retrieval.
questions.r: Slide 11: stemming shortens words mechanically with affix rules and may yield non-words; lemmatisation uses morphology and often context to give the dictionary lemma.

questions.q: In "Wiele mam nie przyszło", the analyser lists mama, mieć and mamić for mam. What does the tagger do?
o: Chooses the reading that fits the context
Corrects the spelling of the word
Removes the word from the sentence
questions.hint: Analysis aims for coverage; tagging for the right choice.
questions.r: Slides 12–13: the analyser proposes all candidates; the tagger selects mama, noun, genitive plural, because the context means "many mothers did not come".

questions.q: In the tag subst:pl:inst:m2 for kotami, what does inst mean?
questions.hint: Polish has seven cases.
questions.r: Slide 14: subst = noun, pl = plural, inst = instrumental case, m2 = masculine animate gender class.

questions.q: With BIO labels, how is "New York University" tagged as an organisation?
questions.hint: Begin once, then continue.
questions.r: Slide 18: B-type begins an entity, I-type continues it, O is outside; the three tokens are B-ORG I-ORG I-ORG.

questions.q: Ocean, sea and body of water: which pairing is right?
o: body of water is the hypernym; sea is a co-hyponym of ocean
ocean is the hypernym of body of water and of sea
sea is the hypernym; ocean is its meronym
body of water is a meronym of ocean and of sea
questions.hint: An ocean must be a body of water.
questions.r: Slide 24: body of water is the more general meaning (hypernym), ocean the more specific (hyponym), and sea another kind under the same hypernym (co-hyponym).

questions.q: "A slice is a portion of bread" is which kind of relation?
questions.hint: Part–whole relations come in subtypes.
questions.r: Slide 25: meronymy covers part, portion, place, collection element and material; slice / bread is the portion subtype.

questions.q: For authorship analysis, which preprocessing step is risky?
questions.hint: Style lives in the details.
questions.r: Slide 29: authorship needs stylistic variation, so spelling correction is risky; for sentiment, removing punctuation is risky; for entity linking, lowercasing everything.

questions.q: Using "Nowak visited New York University", explain how errors propagate through an NLP pipeline.
questions.a:
1. A wrong sentence split changes the context available to later steps.
2. Wrong token boundaries change the units the tagger sees.
3. Wrong tags remove useful grammatical evidence.
4. An NER boundary error splits the organisation name (e.g. New York + University).
5. Entity linking then searches for the wrong object.
Only end-to-end evaluation shows the practical effect of early decisions.

questions.q: Which of these is a hyperparameter rather than a learned parameter?
o: A weight in a hidden layer
A bias of an output neuron
A coefficient of a linear model
questions.hint: It is chosen outside parameter training.
questions.r: Slide 4: weights, biases and coefficients are learned from training data; learning rate, regularisation and layer sizes are hyperparameters chosen with validation.

questions.q: What must the test set not be used for?
questions.hint: That is the validation set's job.
questions.r: Slide 6: the test set gives one final estimate on unseen data and must not be used for repeated model selection; validation chooses hyperparameters and stopping time.

questions.q: Which practice causes data leakage?
o: Estimating IDF on all documents, test set included
Splitting the data by author or by customer
Using a later time period as the test set
Fitting preprocessing on the training data only
questions.hint: Statistics from the test data must not reach training.
questions.r: Slide 7: using non-training documents to build the vocabulary or estimate IDF leaks information; the other options are the safer grouping practices.

questions.q: With TP = 80, FN = 20, FP = 10 and TN = 890, what is the recall for spam?
questions.hint: TP / (TP + FN).

questions.q: Precision answers which question?
o: When the model says spam, how often is it right?
Of all spam messages, how many were found?
How many messages were classified correctly?
How balanced are precision and recall?
questions.hint: It looks at the predicted positives.
questions.r: Slide 14: precision = TP / (TP + FP); recall is the share of all spam found; accuracy counts all correct decisions; F1 balances precision and recall.

questions.q: One percent of messages are fraud and a model always predicts "not fraud". What are its accuracy and fraud recall?
questions.hint: It never finds a single fraud.
questions.r: Slide 15: accuracy is 99% but fraud recall is 0%, which is why per-class results matter when some classes are rare.

questions.q: Which averaging gives every class equal importance?
questions.hint: The other one aggregates all decisions together.
questions.r: Slide 15: macro averaging gives every class equal importance; micro averaging aggregates decisions and favours frequent classes.

questions.q: A document can carry several tags at once. Which output layer fits?
questions.hint: Softmax assumes exactly one class.
questions.r: Slide 21: binary uses one sigmoid; multiclass one softmax (probabilities sum to one, exclusive classes); multilabel one sigmoid per label.

questions.q: If the probability of the correct class is 0.1, what is the cross-entropy loss −log py?
questions.r: Slide 22: −log 0.1 ≈ 2.303 (squared error (1 − 0.1)² = 0.81). At 0.9 the loss is 0.105 and at 0.5 it is 0.693: confident mistakes cost much more.

questions.q: Why do hidden layers need nonlinear activations?
o: Stacked linear layers collapse into one linear map
Nonlinear functions make training data larger
Linear layers cannot have bias terms
ReLU keeps all outputs between 0 and 1
questions.hint: A product of matrices is still a matrix.
questions.r: Slide 17: without nonlinearity, several linear layers equal one linear transformation; ReLU = max(0, z) is unbounded above, sigmoid maps to (0, 1).

questions.q: Which statement about support vector machines is true?
o: They prefer the boundary with the largest margin
Their raw scores are calibrated probabilities
They cannot handle large sparse vocabularies
Every training example is a support vector
questions.hint: Support vectors are the closest examples.
questions.r: Slide 12: an SVM favours a large-margin boundary; support vectors are the examples nearest to it; a linear SVM scales to large TF–IDF vocabularies; raw scores are not probabilities.

questions.q: Why do "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" get the same bag-of-words vector?
o: Bag of words keeps counts but loses order
Both sentences have the same sentiment
The vocabulary removes all frequent words
Character n-grams merge the two words
questions.hint: Each word occurs once in both.
questions.r: Slide 28: bag of words keeps term presence and frequency but discards global word order, syntax and discourse structure.

questions.q: What do word bigrams such as "not good" add to a bag-of-words model?
questions.hint: At the cost of a much bigger vocabulary.
questions.r: Slide 29: word n-grams capture phrases and negation; character n-grams tolerate spelling variation; both enlarge the vocabulary dramatically.

questions.q: For the spam filter with TP = 80, FN = 20, FP = 10, TN = 890, compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1, and say what a false positive means here.
questions.a:
- Accuracy = (80 + 890) / 1000 = 0.97
- Precision = 80 / (80 + 10) ≈ 0.889
- Recall = 80 / (80 + 20) = 0.80
- F1 = 2 · 0.889 · 0.80 / (0.889 + 0.80) ≈ 0.842
A false positive is a legitimate message blocked as spam.
